title: THE LOVERS HEAR EACH OTHER, SEARCH FOR EACH OTHER, MISS EACH OTHER, AND LONG FOR EACH OTHER—BIBLICAL ROMANCE IS NOT EMOTIONLESS
paragraphs: THE LOVERS HEAR EACH OTHER, SEARCH FOR EACH OTHER, MISS EACH OTHER, AND LONG FOR EACH OTHER—BIBLICAL ROMANCE IS NOT EMOTIONLESS
Somewhere along the way, some Christians became so afraid of lust that they almost became afraid of love. But Scripture never was.
There is a woman awake at night because the man she loves is absent.
She reaches for him.
He is not there.
She searches.
She cannot find him.
She gets up.
She walks through the city.
She asks the watchmen if they have seen him.
Why?
Because she misses him.
Because love has made absence painful.
And somehow this scene is sitting right there in the Bible.
Not in a secular romance novel.
Not in a Hollywood screenplay.
Not in a forbidden diary somebody hid beneath a mattress.
In Scripture.
The Song of Songs gives us these startling Hebrew words:
עַל־מִשְׁכָּבִי בַּלֵּילוֹת בִּקַּשְׁתִּי אֵת שֶׁאָהֲבָה נַפְשִׁי
ʿal-mishkavi balleilot biqqashti et she’ahavah nafshi…
“On my bed at night, I sought the one whom my soul loves…”
Then comes the ache:
בִּקַּשְׁתִּיו וְלֹא מְצָאתִיו
“I sought him, but I did not find him.”
—Song of Songs 3:1
Read that slowly.
The one whom my soul loves.
She misses him.
She searches for him.
She longs to find him.
And God did not blush and remove those words from His Bible.
Maybe we should stop pretending biblical romance is emotionless.
Because sometimes Christians have been taught a strange version of love.
Be committed—but do not be too emotional.
Be faithful—but do not be too passionate.
Marry—but somehow pretend attraction does not matter.
Love your spouse—but never speak as though you actually ache for their presence.
Desire marriage—but feel vaguely guilty for wanting to be wanted.
We rightly warn people against lust.
We rightly warn against sexual immorality.
We rightly preach holiness.
But holiness does not require emotional anesthesia.
Purity is not the absence of affection.
Biblical self-control is not the death of tenderness.
And godly romance is not two Christians signing a theological contract and then spending fifty years pretending they never desperately wanted to hold each other.
The Bible is far more human than that.
The lovers hear each other.
They search for each other.
They miss each other.
They admire each other.
They delight in each other.
They long for each other.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs permission to understand something:
Wanting to be deeply loved is not automatically carnality.
The problem is not that the human heart longs to love.
The problem is what sin does with that longing.
There is a difference.
Long before Song of Songs, there was another scene.
A man sees a woman.
And something happens inside him.
Genesis says that when God brought the woman to Adam, Adam responded:
זֹאת הַפַּעַם עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי וּבָשָׂר מִבְּשָׂרִי
Zot happaʿam, ʿetsem meʿatsamai uvasar mibbesari.
“This one, at last, is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”
—Genesis 2:23
Do not miss those little words:
“At last.”
There is recognition there.
Wonder.
Arrival.
Someone corresponding to him.
Then Scripture gives us the foundation of marriage:
A man leaves father and mother, clings to his wife, and the two become one flesh.
Before betrayal entered Eden…
before lust distorted desire…
before pornography commercialized bodies…
before adultery shattered homes…
before manipulation turned affection into leverage…
before people learned to use sex without covenant and covenant without tenderness…
God created man and woman.
Marriage was not Satan's invention.
Romantic love was not Hollywood's invention.
Human sexuality was not invented by pornography.
The enemy did not create these gifts.
He corrupted them.
And there is an enormous difference between creation and corruption.
Maybe that is why Song of Songs can sound almost shocking to ears accustomed to treating Christianity as emotionally sterile.
Listen.
The woman hears something.
קוֹל דּוֹדִי
Qol dodi.
“The voice of my beloved!”
—Song of Songs 2:8
You can almost hear the excitement.
He is coming.
The beloved approaches, and then she remembers his voice calling her:
קוּמִי לָךְ רַעְיָתִי יָפָתִי וּלְכִי־לָךְ
Qumi lakh, raʿyati, yafati, uleki-lakh.
“Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.”
—Song of Songs 2:10
That is not cold.
That is not mechanical.
That is not embarrassed affection.
The lovers speak.
They listen.
They notice.
They praise.
They desire presence.
They experience separation.
They experience reunion.
And sometimes they experience pain.
That matters.
Because maybe you know exactly what it means to miss somebody.
Maybe there is a name you still cannot hear casually.
Maybe there is a chair that became painful after someone left.
Maybe there are photographs you avoid because one image can resurrect an entire season.
Maybe you loved somebody who did not stay.
Maybe your marriage has become painfully quiet.
Maybe you sleep beside someone who feels a thousand miles away.
Maybe you are single, and underneath all the Christian language about “waiting on God's timing,” there are nights when you simply wish somebody would choose you.
Not use you.
Not hide you.
Not keep you as an option.
Choose you.
Maybe you are divorced.
Maybe betrayed.
Maybe widowed.
Maybe still recovering from a relationship where the person who said “I love you” slowly taught you to fear love.
And perhaps you have wondered whether your longing itself was shameful.
Scripture gives us a better answer.
Longing can be beautiful.
But longing also needs redemption.
Because we can turn a person into a god.
We can ask another human being to heal wounds only Christ can reach.
We can demand from romance what romance was never designed to provide.
We can call obsession “love.”
We can call possession “protection.”
We can call lust “chemistry.”
We can call emotional dependency “soulmates.”
We can ignore character because somebody makes our heart race.
We can stay where God is being dishonored because loneliness frightens us more than compromise.
And that is where biblical romance confronts modern romance.
The Bible celebrates love without worshiping the lover.
It celebrates desire without making desire sovereign.
It celebrates the body without separating the body from covenant, faithfulness, holiness, and responsibility.
It allows lovers to burn with affection while still insisting that God remains God.
That distinction can save your heart.
Because no husband can be Jesus.
No wife can be Jesus.
No boyfriend can be Jesus.
No girlfriend can be Jesus.
No wedding can resurrect your soul.
No human kiss can permanently silence the deepest cry inside fallen humanity.
You were created for relationship with people, yes.
But beneath every human hunger is a deeper reality:
You were created for God.
And this is where the love story becomes bigger than romance.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to teach lonely people how to find partners.
He came to rescue sinners.
He came for adulterers.
For the sexually broken.
For the abandoned.
For the ashamed.
For the lustful.
For the betrayed.
For the betrayer who repents.
For the person who gave too much away.
For the person who took what was not theirs.
For the person carrying memories they desperately wish they could erase.
For the person whose private search history would humiliate them if exposed.
For the woman who thinks her past made her unlovable.
For the man who thinks his failures permanently disqualified him.
Christ came into the scandal.
And He brought grace.
Not cheap grace that says sin does not matter.
Grace that tells the truth about sin and then pays an unimaginable price to redeem the sinner.
At the cross, Jesus did not pretend our corruption was beautiful.
He bore it.
The Greek New Testament announces the heart of the Gospel with words Christians should never become numb to:
Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανεν
Christos hyper hēmōn apethanen.
“Christ died for us.”
See Romans 5:8.
While we were still sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we became worthy romantic partners.
Not after we finally stopped struggling.
Christ moved toward sinners.
The Gospel is not the story of good people climbing toward God.
It is the story of the holy Son of God coming down to rescue people who could never save themselves.
That changes romance too.
Because when Christ becomes the center, love stops asking only:
“What can you make me feel?”
Love begins asking:
“How can I honor Christ in the way I treat you?”
That changes dating.
That changes marriage.
That changes sexuality.
That changes conflict.
That changes forgiveness.
That changes attraction.
That changes what you tolerate.
That changes what you refuse.
Biblical love is deeply emotional, but it is more than emotion.
Feelings can say, “I want you.”
Covenant says, “I will be faithful.”
Attraction can say, “You are beautiful.”
Love says, “Your soul matters to God.”
Lust asks, “How much of you can I take?”
Love asks, “How faithfully can I seek your good?”
Manipulation says, “Prove that you love me.”
Godly affection says, “I refuse to make you sin in order to keep me.”
That is romance redeemed.
And Song of Songs gives us perhaps its most unforgettable declaration:
כִּי־עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה
Ki ʿazzah khammavet ahavah.
“For love is strong as death.”
—Song of Songs 8:6
The poem continues with imagery of blazing fire and an astonishing declaration:
Many waters cannot extinguish love.
Floods cannot sweep it away.
That is powerful language.
But Scripture never tells us that every intense feeling is therefore holy.
Intensity alone proves nothing.
You can intensely desire the wrong person.
You can intensely desire someone else's spouse.
You can intensely desire what God has forbidden.
You can intensely miss somebody God rescued you from.
Your tears do not automatically make a relationship righteous.
Your chemistry does not rewrite Scripture.
Your loneliness does not turn disobedience into God's will.
That may hurt.
But sometimes grace hurts before it heals.
Sometimes Jesus loves us enough to separate us from the thing we kept calling love because He can see what it is doing to our souls.
And maybe this article found you while you are trying to return to someone you know keeps pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe you keep rereading messages.
Checking whether they are online.
Remembering the nights when everything felt alive.
Missing the person so badly that you have started editing the memories.
You remember the tenderness.
You forget the compromise.
You remember being held.
You forget how often you were spiritually disappearing.
You remember the apology.
You forget the cycle.
You remember what they promised.
You forget what they repeatedly chose.
Listen carefully:
Missing someone does not always mean you are supposed to return to them.
Sometimes grief is simply the price of finally walking away from what was destroying you.
And sometimes the person you need to run toward is not the person you lost.
It is Jesus.
Because there is another voice in Scripture calling.
Christ describes Himself as the Good Shepherd, and He says His sheep hear His voice.
He knows them.
They follow Him.
See John 10:27.
Do you see the deeper beauty?
The lovers hear each other.
But above every human voice, the redeemed learn to recognize the voice of Christ.
The lovers search for each other.
But Jesus spoke of the shepherd who searches for the lost.
The lovers ache in separation.
But sin created the separation no human romance can ultimately repair.
And the Gospel announces that God acted.
Christ came.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ calls.
Christ forgives.
Christ restores.
Christ makes sinners new.
That is why Christian romance cannot ultimately be about finding somebody who “completes” you.
Christ is not the missing decoration around your love story.
He is Lord.
And when two people belong to Him, romance can become something beautiful precisely because it is no longer required to become their god.
You can say, “I miss you,” without saying, “I cannot exist without you.”
You can say, “I desire you,” without saying, “Therefore I am entitled to you.”
You can say, “You are beautiful,” without turning a body into an object.
You can say, “Stay,” while still surrendering the future to God.
You can love fiercely and worship Christ supremely.
That is freedom.
And married couples, perhaps you need to hear this too.
Do not become so familiar with your spouse that you stop pursuing the person you once prayed God would give you.
Speak.
Listen.
Notice.
Flirt with your spouse.
Tell them they are beautiful.
Tell him you appreciate him.
Tell her what you still notice.
Reach for the hand you have held ten thousand times.
Put the phone down.
Look into the face across the table.
Ask what is happening inside their heart.
Pray together even when it feels awkward.
Repent quickly.
Forgive biblically.
Protect your marriage from secret appetites.
And please—do not outsource to strangers on a screen the desire that belongs inside your covenant.
Pornography trains the eyes to consume bodies without covenant.
Jesus teaches us to see people as souls bearing God's image.
Adultery says desire outranks faithfulness.
Christ teaches us that obedience sometimes means crucifying desires that feel overwhelmingly alive.
Christian marriage does not destroy passion.
It gives passion a holy home.
And single believer, your life is not God's waiting room.
You are not half a Christian until somebody puts a ring on your finger.
Jesus was not incomplete.
Paul was not spiritually defective.
Marriage is a gift.
Singleness can also be a gift.
And neither marital status determines your worth before God.
So do not marry simply because silence scares you.
Do not accept spiritual incompatibility because the attention feels intoxicating.
Do not trade conviction for companionship.
Do not hand your future to someone who wants your body but resents your devotion to Jesus.
You are not looking merely for someone who makes your heart beat faster.
You need character.
Truth.
Repentance.
Faithfulness.
Humility.
Someone who understands that love must eventually survive mornings when nobody feels cinematic.
Because real biblical romance is not less emotional than the world's version.
It is deeper.
It has butterflies, but it cannot survive on butterflies.
It has desire, but desire bows to holiness.
It has tenderness, but tenderness grows backbone.
It has longing, but longing refuses idolatry.
It has passion, but passion learns covenant.
It has forgiveness, but forgiveness never calls evil good.
It has sacrifice.
Patience.
Repentance.
Truth.
Grace.
And Christ at the center.
Maybe that is what your heart has actually been looking for.
Not emotionless Christianity.
Not reckless passion.
Redeemed love.
Love that can look another human being in the eyes and say:
“I desire you, but I will not worship you.”
“I love you, but I will not help you rebel against God.”
“I want you close, but I want Jesus honored more.”
“I will tell you the truth because your soul matters more than my comfort.”
And perhaps the most romantic thing a Christian can ever say is not merely:
“I cannot live without you.”
Maybe it is:
“I want to walk with you toward Jesus.”
Because eventually every beautiful face ages.
Bodies change.
Circumstances collapse.
Money disappears.
Illness comes.
Feelings fluctuate.
And unless Christ returns first, one lover may eventually stand beside the grave of the other.
That sounds unbearable.
Because love makes loss expensive.
But Christians grieve differently because death does not get the final sentence.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
And those who belong to Him possess a hope stronger than the cemetery.
Christian love can stare at mortality without surrendering to despair because the Gospel declares that Jesus rewrites endings.
That is why this message matters.
Maybe somebody on your Facebook friends list has almost given up on love.
Maybe somebody is confusing lust with intimacy.
Maybe somebody is about to return to an abusive or spiritually destructive relationship simply because loneliness became unbearable.
Maybe a married couple is quietly drifting apart.
Maybe a young believer has never been told that attraction is not automatically dirty but must be surrendered to Christ.
Maybe someone feels permanently stained by sexual sin and desperately needs to know that repentance and the blood of Jesus are stronger than their past.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody you know may need truth tonight.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, do not pretend it did not.
You do not have to tell strangers every detail.
Sometimes three words are enough to stop hiding.
Because feelings have short memories.
There may come a night when loneliness starts rewriting history, when temptation starts negotiating with conviction, or when disappointment whispers that biblical love does not exist.
Come back.
Read it again.
Remember what love is supposed to bow before.
Jesus Christ.

Invite your family.

Let them encounter Jesus.
But the greatest reason to stay close is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Truth.
Conviction.
Encouragement.
Accountability.
Spiritual sharpening.
And comment—not for empty engagement, but because your testimony, confession, prayer request, or declaration of faith may become the sentence another wounded person needed to see.
Because biblical romance was never emotionless.
The lovers hear each other.
They search for each other.
They miss each other.
They long for each other.
They delight in each other.
But redeemed love eventually learns something even greater:
No human being was ever meant to carry the weight of being your Savior.
So love deeply.
Desire faithfully.
Guard your heart wisely.
Honor marriage.
Flee sexual immorality.
Repent when you fall.
Forgive as Christ teaches.
Refuse counterfeit intimacy.
And never make an idol out of the person whose hand you hope to hold.
Hold their hand.
But give Jesus your throne.

Because after every heartbreak, every betrayal, every lonely night, every sinful chapter, every shattered expectation, every tear on the pillow, and every scandal you thought permanently ruined the story, there remains a Savior with nail-scarred hands who still knows how to write redemption.
And sometimes the heart spends years searching for someone to love it perfectly before discovering that Perfect Love had been calling its name all along.
